Adolescent Kyphosis

flexible and structural roundback · vertebral wedging · growth and progression

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Adolescent roundback: a curve that corrects with extension or a change of position is postural; a rigid curve needs spinal radiographs for Scheuermann disease (Scheuermann kyphosis).
  • Anterior wedging of at least 5 degrees in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae supports Scheuermann disease. Use the curve, progression, symptoms and growth remaining to plan treatment.
  • Mild, stable curve: conservative care. Progressing curve with growth remaining: consider a brace. Refractory pain, neurologic impairment or severe deformity: orthopedic assessment for intervention.
What it is

Structural kyphosis from abnormal vertebral growth during adolescence

Driver

The cause is uncertain; vertebral endplate growth is disturbed

Triggers

Adolescent growth; boys somewhat more often affected (non-modifiable)

Some cases run in families (non-modifiable)

Chain

Endplate disturbance anterior vertebral wedging a rigid forward curve

Insights

Test flexibility before interpreting the film. Postural roundback corrects; a structural deformity does not.

Growth changes the treatment. Bracing is used for a growing child whose curve increases; persistent severe symptoms require a different discussion.

2Urgent risks
Red flagsNight pain, weight loss, neurologic changes or systemic illness

If the presentation is atypical for uncomplicated kyphosis, choose evaluate promptly for tumor, infection or neural compression; obtain MRI as indicated.

Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy with 1 year of worsening thoracic roundback aching mid-back pain curve does not correct prone or in extension No morning stiffness or buttock pain Afebrile · lateral film: 8-degree anterior wedging of 3 consecutive mid-thoracic vertebrae, Schmorl nodes → Scheuermann disease → Rigidity and anterior wedging of at least 5 degrees across three adjacent vertebrae support Scheuermann disease; postural kyphosis is flexible.
  2. 15-year-old girl whose parents worry about her upper back round shoulders for 2 years curve fully corrects lying prone and on active extension No back pain Afebrile · lateral film: smooth curve, no vertebral wedging → Postural kyphosis → A fully correctable curve without vertebral wedging is postural kyphosis; exercises and reassurance are appropriate.
  3. 16-year-old boy with 8 months of increasing thoracic roundback mild mid-back ache after sports curve does not correct in hyperextension No pain that wakes him from sleep or weight loss Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Standing lateral thoracic spine radiograph → Standing spinal radiographs establish vertebral shape and the curve angle. MRI is used for an atypical presentation, neurologic findings or concern for another lesion.
  4. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease 1 year ago Cobb angle now 65 degrees, up from 52 about 2 years of growth remaining Doing his extension exercises Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Brace until skeletal maturity → The curve has progressed with growth still remaining, so bracing is appropriate. Surgical assessment is for severe disease or symptoms that resist nonoperative care.
  5. 17-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease at 13 Cobb angle 80 degrees skeletally mature; physes closed on film Back pain limits school despite a year of physical therapy Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Posterior spinal fusion → The skeleton is mature and pain remains disabling after prolonged physical therapy. Surgical assessment for corrective fusion is appropriate.
Transferable rule

Whether the curve corrects with extension separates structural from postural kyphosis; radiographs confirm the vertebral pattern.
